title: Education Christodoulou, Daisy Why Personalising Education Based on Student Interests Doesn't Work
author: Christodoulou, Daisy
summary: Christodoulou challenges the claim that LLMs will transform education by enabling interest-based personalized learning, arguing this rests on a misunderstanding of how analogies and prior knowledge work. The case for interest personalization is that we learn new things by connecting them to old things, so tailored resources should help. But this fails for two reasons: first, a good analogy requires something the student already knows very well -- if you have to explain the comparison, it has failed; second, analogies must be chosen based on what works for the content, not the learner's preference, just as learning styles fail because preferences cannot override the inherent modality of the task. She concedes there is a workable form of AI personalization: students progressing through shared content at different speeds based on performance, not student choice.
points: * Interest-based personalization is a bait-and-switch: the problem it claims to solve ('my teacher went too fast') is not solved by having students demonstrate equations in the style of a cooking show -- the stated problem requires re-explanation, not creative reframing. * The first principle of a good analogy is that the comparison must involve something students already understand very well; if you have to explain what a plumber does first, the analogy has failed -- it is now a distraction. * The second principle is that analogies must be chosen based on the content, not learner's preference -- the same logic behind why learning styles don't work: you can't choose to learn a map of Africa through a podcast. * Most students have limited prior knowledge, which severely constrains the pool of viable analogies. * A workable form of AI personalization exists: students progressing through shared compulsory content at different speeds based on performance rather than student choice.
quotes: I am pretty dubious about personalised education. I wrote a long chapter about it in my 2020 book Teachers vs Tech, where I argued that most forms of personalisation don't work.
I have also found that many advocates of personalisation rely on a sleight-of-hand. They will start out by asking if, when you were a student, you felt that the pace of a class was too fast or slow.

This is a complete bait-and-switch! If the problem is 'my maths teacher went too fast and I wish they could repeat that middle step again' the solution is not 'demonstrate how to solve equations with iMovie videos in the style of a cooking show.'
And that's lesson one of creating a good analogy. If you have to explain the thing you're comparing it to, it's failed. It's serving not as an explanation, but a distraction.

The reason why learning styles don't work is because you have to pick the style based on the content, not the learner's preference! If you want to learn where the countries are on a map of Africa, that is just inherently a visual task.
When students express an interest in football, they tend not to mean 'I want to hear your hand-crafted analogy about the Old Firm's religious selection policies.'
All models are wrong, but some are useful. I would update it with: and some are useless!
